subject: HarborBank private access — ingress approach, NATting & auth patterns
messages:
From: Alex Morgan <alex.morgan@harborbank.com>
To: Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwood.com>
Cc: Hannah Schmitt <hannah_schmitt@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 20 Jul 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Ingress options — overlap, NAT and auth concerns (HarborBank)

Connor,

Thanks for the call this morning. We sketched the network overlay and I attached the current topology (harbor_net_topology_v2.pdf). A few implementation constraints to surface before you recommend a path: 

- We have overlapping RFC1918 ranges with a couple of legacy on-prem clusters (10.0.0.0/16 used in two datacenters).
- Our security team requires mutual auth (mTLS) for any persistent tunnel; IP allowlists alone are not acceptable for production.
- We need predictable egress IPs for compliance (we use a set of IPs on an allowlist with our downstream partners).
- We want minimal operational blast radius — ideally a single connectivity mode for the production fleet, but can accept a staged approach.

Can you outline the tradeoffs between: (A) VPC peering (B) AWS PrivateLink / interface endpoints (C) site-to-site VPN (managed) — specifically with respect to NATting, mTLS, and how we preserve static egress IPs? Also include any temporary stopgap we could use while we complete IP renumbering.

Appreciate a short options table and an ask list for NetOps/procurement.

Thanks,
Alex
---
Alex Morgan
Sr. Manager, Network Engineering
HarborBank
netops@harborbank.com

Attachment: harbor_net_topology_v2.pdf (diagram, 1.2MB)

From: Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwood.com>
To: Alex Morgan <alex.morgan@harborbank.com>
Cc: Hannah Schmitt <hannah_schmitt@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 20 Jul 2026 12:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Ingress options — overlap, NAT and auth concerns (HarborBank)

Alex — thanks for the clear constraints and the diagram; that's very helpful. High-level summary up front, then a short matrix and recommended next steps.

Short summary: 
- VPC peering: lowest-latency, simplest path for non-overlapping IPs. Does not support cross-account interface endpoints for private services; no built-in mTLS layer — you'd implement mTLS at the application or LB. NATting to preserve your static egress IPs requires a managed NAT gateway in the peered VPC or egress through a transit appliance. Not ideal if you cannot renumber.

- PrivateLink / Interface Endpoints: best for per-service access without route table changes and handles overlapping IP spaces because traffic terminates at an ENI in your account. PrivateLink preserves source IPs only to the extent of the endpoint; for predictable egress IPs you still need an egress NAT path under your control (e.g., a dedicated NAT gateway or egress proxy in HarborBank account). PrivateLink allows you to centralize mTLS at the service front door (we can terminate or pass-through) and can be combined with AWS Private CA for certs.

- Site-to-site VPN (managed): fastest to stand up and works with overlapping ranges when combined with NAT. It gives you full network visibility but is the least granular and can be brittle at scale. For mTLS, you can run mTLS over the tunnel at the application or terminate at an internal LB. Predictable egress IPs are achievable by hairpinning traffic through your egress NATs, but that increases latency.

Quick 3-row matrix (latency | overlap-friendly | mTLS-friendly | static-egress-friendly | ops burden):
- VPC peering: Low | No | App-level only | Medium (requires NAT) | Low
- PrivateLink: Low-Medium | Yes | Very (good for service auth) | High (you manage egress) | Medium
- S2S VPN: Medium-High | Yes (with NAT) | App-level only | High or Medium (depending on hairpin/NAT) | Medium-High

Recommended pattern for HarborBank (short):
1) Short-term (90 days): Managed site-to-site VPN with a small NAT translation rule set to avoid renumbering immediately. This gets you secure connectivity quickly and lets your security team validate mTLS at the app layer.
2) Medium-term (3–6 months): Implement PrivateLink for our private service endpoints (customer-specific interface endpoints) for services where we need strict service-level auth and per-service ACLs. PrivateLink avoids your IP overlap issues and is the cleanest model for RBAC + mTLS at the front door.
3) Long-term (>6 months): When you finish renumbering, prefer peering for latency-sensitive bulk traffic and use PrivateLink for control-plane/service-plane access.

Ask list for your NetOps/procurement team (what we need from you):
- Confirmation of which HarborBank account(s) will host the egress NAT/proxy (account IDs and expected public IPs).
- A list of current RFC1918 ranges and any flexibility window for renumbering.
- Certificate management preference (do you use AWS Private CA, Vault, or your PKI?).
- If going PrivateLink: contact for the AWS account that will create interface endpoints and any Service Consumer whitelisting requirements.
- If going S2S VPN: preferred managed vendor (e.g., AWS VPN vs. third-party) and whether you want BGP or static.

I'll attach a short matrix (redwood_private_connectivity_matrix.xlsx) and a brief outline we can use in the SOC / network review. Propose a 30m follow-up with your NetOps + Security to lock the stopgap and the medium-term plan.

Connor
Principal Solutions Engineer
Redwood Inference
connor_obrien@redwood.com

Attachment: redwood_private_connectivity_matrix.xlsx (spreadsheet, 80KB)

From: Hannah Schmitt <hannah_schmitt@redwood.com>
To: Alex Morgan <alex.morgan@harborbank.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 21 Jul 2026 10:18:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Ingress options — overlap, NAT and auth concerns (HarborBank)

Alex — quick operational notes from an SRE/security standpoint: 

- mTLS: we recommend terminating mTLS at a fronting TLS proxy (in your account if using PrivateLink, or in a customer-managed ingress ELB if peering) so your security team can manage cert rotation and CRL/OCSP checks. We can provide scripts for automated cert rotation if you have a Vault/PKI.
- NAT strategy: If you must keep your current ranges, plan for a small NAT stage (20–50 rules) rather than full renumbering. Use an egress proxy (squid/nginx) behind an EIP pool to provide static IPs rather than per-instance NAT gateways — it makes allowlisting easier and is auditable.
- MTU & fragmentation: watch for PMTU issues over VPN (we've seen APP-layer failures when PMTU drops below ~1300). Recommend TCP MSS clamping on the tunnel or set MTU 1400 on the appliance.

Stopgap recommendation aligns with Connor: short-term managed VPN + NAT egress proxy. We can support an interim config that maps a small set of internal ranges and returns traffic through your egress proxies so downstream partners see stable IPs.

I can prepare a short runbook for the interim approach (what NetOps changes, what we change on Redwood side, test plan) if you want — estimate 4–6 engineering hours to validate and test.

-Hannah
Sr. SRE, Redwood Inference
